paragraphs: Based on current CMS guidelines and Medicare rules
Each question has one best answer based on Medicare Advantage rules.
Choose A, B, C, or D
Select the option that most accurately answers the question.
Note your responses; the full Answer Key appears at the end.
Use the answer key with brief explanations to reinforce knowledge.
What is Medicare Advantage (MA) also known as?
To enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan, a person must have:
Both Part A and Part B
Private insurance companies that contract with Medicare
Most Medicare Advantage plans include which additional coverage?
What is a key difference between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage regarding out-of-pocket costs?
Original Medicare has a yearly out-of-pocket maximum
Medicare Advantage plans must have an annual out-of-pocket maximum
Only Part D has an out-of-pocket limit
In 2025, the federal maximum out-of-pocket limit (MOOP) for in-network services in MA plans was set at approximately:
Which type of Medicare Advantage plan typically requires members to use in-network providers and often needs referrals for specialists?
Can a person with Medicare Advantage also purchase a Medigap (Medicare Supplement) policy?
No, Medigap cannot be used with Medicare Advantage
Only if the MA plan is an HMO
What is the Annual Coordinated Election Period (AEP) for Medicare Advantage?
During the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (MA OEP), what can beneficiaries do?
Only switch from Original Medicare to MA
Switch MA plans or return to Original Medicare (Jan 1 – March 31)
Enroll in any Medigap plan without underwriting
Approximately what percentage of eligible Medicare beneficiaries were enrolled in Medicare Advantage in recent years (2025–2026)?
Many Medicare Advantage plans offer supplemental benefits not covered by Original Medicare. Which of the following is commonly offered?
How are Medicare Advantage plans primarily paid by Medicare?
Only when claims are submitted by the member
What is a Special Needs Plan (SNP)?
A plan only for people under 65
An MA plan designed for people with specific conditions or dual eligibility
A plan that covers only Part D
Which of the following is true about provider networks in Medicare Advantage?
All MA plans allow any Medicare provider nationwide
HMO plans usually limit care to in-network providers
PPO plans never cover out-of-network care
Networks are the same as Original Medicare
If a Medicare Advantage member needs emergency care while traveling outside the plan’s service area, what typically happens?
Emergency and urgently needed care is covered
The member must pay 100% and seek reimbursement later
What is the main purpose of the Medicare Advantage rebate?
Funds that plans can use to lower premiums, reduce cost-sharing, or offer supplemental benefits
Can a person who has End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan?
Yes, under current rules (restrictions largely lifted)
What does “zero-premium” Medicare Advantage plan usually mean?
The plan covers the Part B premium completely and charges $0
The enrollee pays $0 for the MA plan premium (still pays Part B premium)
Which statement about prior authorization in Medicare Advantage is generally true?
Many MA plans use prior authorization for certain services
Only Original Medicare uses prior authorization
Prior authorization is illegal under CMS rules
If a beneficiary is enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan and needs hospice care, who primarily covers the hospice services?
Original Medicare (hospice is covered by Original Medicare)
What is the typical structure of cost-sharing in many Medicare Advantage HMO plans?
Fixed copayments for office visits and services
During which period can a newly eligible Medicare beneficiary first enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan?
During their Initial Coverage Election Period (ICEP)
Which of the following is a common reason someone might prefer Original Medicare over Medicare Advantage?
Desire for a broad nationwide provider choice without network restrictions
Wanting extra dental and vision benefits
What happens if a Medicare Advantage plan leaves the market or the enrollee moves out of the service area?
The person is locked into the plan forever
A Special Enrollment Period (SEP) is typically available
Coverage ends immediately with no options
They must wait until the next AEP only
Which organization sets the rules and oversees Medicare Advantage plans?
In a Medicare Advantage PPO plan, what is generally true about out-of-network care?
It is usually covered but often at higher cost-sharing
It requires a referral from the primary care doctor
A plan for people with diabetes only
A Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan for those with both Medicare and Medicaid
A plan that only covers drugs
Approximately what share of individual Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage charged $0 premium (beyond Part B) in recent years?
Around 75% or more of enrollees are in $0 premium plans
Can Medicare Advantage plans charge higher cost-sharing than Original Medicare for the same service?
They must follow CMS rules and cannot exceed certain limits; overall value must be actuarially equivalent or better
What is the Medicare Advantage Maximum Out-of-Pocket (MOOP) designed to do?
Limit the plan’s payments to providers
Protect enrollees by capping their annual spending on covered Part A and B services
If someone joins a Medicare Advantage plan for the first time and is unhappy, what option do they have in the first 3 months of the year?
Use the MA Open Enrollment Period to switch plans or return to Original Medicare
Which statement best describes Star Ratings for Medicare Advantage plans?
They are purely marketing and have no impact
CMS rates plans 1–5 stars based on quality and performance; higher stars can affect payments and enrollment
Only Part D plans receive Star Ratings
Stars are assigned by the plans themselves
True or False: All Medicare Advantage plans must cover the same core benefits as Original Medicare (Parts A and B).
False – they can exclude hospital care
False – they only cover Part B
True, but only if the member pays extra
What should a beneficiary primarily consider when choosing between Original Medicare and a Medicare Advantage plan?
Provider network, total costs (premiums + cost-sharing), extra benefits, and personal health needs
The color of the plan brochure
Review the correct answers and short explanations
Medicare Advantage is also called Medicare Part C.
Eligibility requires both Medicare Part A and Part B.
Private insurers contract with Medicare to offer MA plans.
Most MA plans are MA-PDs and include Part D drug coverage.
MA plans are required to cap annual out-of-pocket spending for Part A and B services.
CMS set the 2025 in-network MOOP maximum at $9,350.
HMOs generally require in-network care and referrals for specialists.
You cannot have Medigap while enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan.
AEP runs October 15 through December 7 each year.
MA OEP (Jan 1–Mar 31) allows one change: switch MA plans or return to Original Medicare.
Over half (around 54–55%) of eligible beneficiaries are enrolled in MA plans.
Dental, vision, and hearing benefits are very common supplemental benefits in MA plans.
Medicare pays MA plans a fixed monthly amount (capitation) per enrollee.
SNPs serve dual-eligible individuals, those with chronic conditions, or institutionalized beneficiaries.
HMOs generally restrict coverage to their network (with exceptions for emergencies).
MA plans must cover emergency and urgently needed services even out of network/area.
Rebates result when a plan’s bid is below the benchmark; they fund extra benefits or lower costs.
The previous ESRD enrollment restriction was removed; people with ESRD can generally join MA plans.
Zero-premium means $0 additional MA plan premium; the standard Part B premium still applies.
Prior authorization is commonly used by MA plans for certain procedures, DME, and therapies.
Hospice care is covered under Original Medicare even if the person remains in an MA plan.
Many MA plans use set copays (e.g., $20 primary care) rather than 20% coinsurance.
The Initial Coverage Election Period allows first-time enrollment in an MA plan.
Original Medicare allows any provider that accepts Medicare, anywhere in the U.S.
Loss of plan or moving out of area triggers a Special Enrollment Period.
CMS contracts with and regulates Medicare Advantage organizations.
PPOs typically cover out-of-network services at higher cost-sharing levels.
D-SNPs are designed for dual-eligible beneficiaries (Medicare + Medicaid).
A large majority of MA-PD enrollees are in plans with $0 additional premium.
Plans must provide at least the same overall value; individual services have cost-sharing limits set by CMS.
MOOP protects beneficiaries by limiting their annual out-of-pocket costs for covered services.
The MA OEP (January–March) allows one change for those already in MA.
CMS Star Ratings measure quality; higher-rated plans may receive bonus payments and attract more members.
MA plans must cover all medically necessary Part A and Part B services (with limited exceptions such as hospice).
The best choice depends on doctors/hospitals used, expected care needs, travel, and total cost exposure.
You’ve completed the 35-question Medicare Advantage quiz.
Review any missed questions using the Answer Key and stay current with annual CMS updates, as plan rules and benefits can change each year.
